docs.text: Name: Sam Kholmunov Team: Team 102 – Project Aurora Subsystem: Storage Environment

docs.title: My Role
docs.text: I am responsible for the Storage Environment subsystem. This board monitors temperature and light conditions using a thermistor and photodiode. The signals are conditioned using an MCP6002 dual op-amp and processed by the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Name: Sam Kholmuminov Team: Team 102 – Project Aurora Subsystem: Storage Environment (Board D: Temperature & Light) Last updated: October 13, 2026

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
My board is the Storage Environment board in Project Aurora. It watches the temperature and the light level inside the storage area, cleans up the sensor signals with an op-amp, converts them with the ADC on the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, and sends alerts to my teammates over the team's 8-wire ribbon cable.

For every major block in my block diagram I looked at at least three real parts, listed the good and bad points of each, and then picked one.

How I chose (the rules I had to follow):

  • The course gives each team member a $60 budget. The Curiosity Nano and the PCB itself do not count against it.
  • Every part must have a datasheet (no Amazon parts without specifications).
  • Through-hole parts are allowed in EGR 304, so I favored through-hole parts because they are easier to solder and to replace.
  • My board needs a 5 V linear regulator, a barrel jack for a 9 V wall adapter, and a removable fuse.
  • No daughter boards or breakout boards.

docs.title: 1. Light sensor — Storage Environment subsystem (light sensing)
docs.text:
What it has to do: tell the difference between "lights off / box closed" and "lights on / box open" inside the storage area, and give the PIC a smooth analog voltage it can read with its ADC. The light changes slowly (someone opens a door), so speed is not important.

Table 1: Light sensor options

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.NSL-19M51 CdS photocell (light-dependent resistor)Advanced Photonix$1.05 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Very large signal: its resistance swings from about 20 MΩ in the dark to 20–100 kΩ at 10 lux, so a simple divider plus a small op-amp gain gives the ADC a wide, easy-to-read voltage range* Peak sensitivity at 550 nm, which is close to the human eye, so "looks dark to a person" also looks dark to the sensor* Works from 0 V to 5 V with no bias voltage and no special layout; only two leads* Through-hole, 5 mm radial package, easy to solder and easy to mount facing the opening of the storage box* Already used in my Sensor Design schematic, so my KiCad symbol and footprint exist * Slow response (tens of milliseconds), so it cannot measure fast flicker (not a problem for this job)* Resistance drifts a little with temperature Option 2.BPW34 PIN photodiodeVishay$1.37 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Very fast and very linear: output current is proportional to light* Wide 130° viewing angle and a large 7.5 mm² active area* Very low dark current (2 nA), so the "dark" reading is clean* Through-hole, two leads * The signal is a tiny current (microamps indoors), so it needs a transimpedance amplifier with a feedback resistor in the hundreds of kΩ to MΩ range* Peak sensitivity at 900 nm (infrared), so it responds strongly to things people cannot see (warm bulbs, sunlight leaks)* Needs a carefully designed op-amp stage to work well* Most expensive of the three Option 3.TEPT5700 ambient-light phototransistorVishay$1.13 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Built-in gain (it is a transistor), so one resistor turns light into a usable voltage* Peak at 570 nm, filtered to match the human eye* Faster than a photocell * Only 6 V maximum collector-emitter voltage, so there is almost no safety margin on a 5 V board* Narrower 100° viewing angle* Output saturates in bright light, so the useful range is narrow unless the load resistor is tuned carefully

Choice: Option 1, the NSL-19M51 CdS photocell.

Rationale: My job is a simple one: "is the storage area lit or dark, and roughly how bright is it." The photocell gives the biggest signal with the simplest circuit. In the dark its resistance is in the megaohms; under room light it drops to tens of kilohms. That means the divider output (photocell from 5 V, 3.3 kΩ to ground) moves by volts, not millivolts, so the op-amp stage only needs a small gain (about 4) to spread the interesting part of the range across the full 0–5 V ADC input. The photodiode (Option 2) is the more precise sensor, but it would force me to build a transimpedance amplifier with a megaohm feedback resistor, and a circuit like that is sensitive to board leakage, noise and layout mistakes, which is a real risk on a first PCB. The phototransistor (Option 3) is a good middle ground, but its 6 V rating leaves no margin on a 5 V rail and its part-to-part spread is large, so I would have to calibrate every board anyway. The photocell is also the part I already breadboarded and drew in my Sensor Design schematic, so choosing it keeps my schematic, symbol library and footprint library unchanged.

docs.title: 2. Temperature sensor — Storage Environment subsystem (temperature sensing)
docs.text:
What it has to do: report the temperature inside the storage area (roughly 0–50 °C) well enough to raise a temperature alert when it drifts out of range. One degree of accuracy is plenty.

Table 2: Temperature sensor options

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.B57164K0103J000 10 kΩ NTC thermistorTDK (EPCOS)$0.57 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Biggest signal of the three: with a 10 kΩ divider on 5 V the output moves from about 1.6 V at 10 °C to 3.3 V at 40 °C (roughly 58 mV per °C), so no amplifier is needed, only a buffer and a filter* Least expensive option* Two leads, no supply pin, works at any voltage; cannot be damaged by wiring the supply backwards* Wide range (−55 °C to 125 °C) and rated 450 mW, so self-heating from the 0.25 mA divider current is negligible* It is the part already in my team block diagram * Not linear: the PIC must convert the ADC reading with a small lookup table* ±5 % resistance tolerance means about ±1–2 °C error unless I calibrate it once* The fixed divider resistor also adds error, so I should use a 1 % resistor there Option 2.MCP9700A-E/TO analog temperature sensor ICMicrochip$0.61 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Linear output, 10 mV per °C with a 500 mV offset, so the math in code is one line* ±2 °C accuracy with no calibration* Works from 2.3 V to 5.5 V, draws only 6 µA* Through-hole TO-92 package * Small signal: only 0.6 V to 0.9 V over the 10–40 °C range, which uses less than a tenth of the 5 V ADC range unless I add gain* Needs a supply pin, a bypass capacitor and correct polarity Option 3.TMP36GT9Z analog temperature sensor ICAnalog Devices$1.85 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Same simple linear 10 mV per °C output as the MCP9700A* Well-known part with many application notes and example code* 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply, low current, has a shutdown pin * Three times the price of the thermistor for the same job* Same small-signal problem as Option 2 (needs gain to use the ADC range)* ±3 °C accuracy, worse than the MCP9700A* Needs a supply pin and bypass capacitor

Choice: Option 1, the TDK B57164K0103J000 10 kΩ NTC thermistor.

Rationale: The thermistor wins on signal size and on price. With a plain 10 kΩ divider on the 5 V rail, its output changes about 58 mV for every degree, which is almost six times more than the 10 mV per degree from the two IC sensors. That big swing means I do not need any gain for this channel, just one op-amp wired as a unity-gain buffer plus an RC low-pass filter, and the PIC's ADC still gets good resolution (about 0.02 °C per ADC step with the 12-bit ADC). The thermistor's non-linear curve is handled by the B-equation in software (B = 4300 K from the datasheet), which is a few lines of C. Its ±5 % tolerance gives roughly ±1–2 °C of error; that is fine for an alert that triggers when a storage area gets too warm or too cold, and I can calibrate the offset once against a thermometer. Because it is a plain resistor it also cannot be damaged by reversed power and does not need a supply pin or a bypass capacitor.

docs.title: 3. Signal-conditioning op-amp — Storage Environment subsystem (amplifier for both sensors and the DAC output buffer)
docs.text:
What it has to do: I need four op-amp sections: (A) a buffer for the photocell divider, (B) the gain stage for the light signal, (C) a buffer for the thermistor divider, and (D) a buffer for the PIC's DAC output that sends the analog temperature level signal to my teammates on ribbon-cable pin 6. All of them run from the single 5 V rail and must swing close to 0 V and 5 V so the PIC's ADC and my teammates' ADCs see the full range.

Table 3: Op-amp options

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.MCP6004-I/P quad op-amp, 14-pin DIPMicrochip$0.60 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Four op-amps in one chip: all four stages I need fit in one 14-pin package with one bypass capacitor* Rail-to-rail input and output: on a 5 V supply the output really goes from about 0 V to 5 V, so no ADC range is wasted* 1 pA input bias current, so it does not load the high-impedance photocell and thermistor dividers* Single supply 1.8 V to 6 V, only 100 µA per amplifier* 1 MHz bandwidth, more than enough for slow sensor signals* Through-hole DIP, can go in a socket; it is the part already in my Sensor Design schematic * 6 V absolute maximum supply, so it can never be run from 9 V by mistake (the 5 V rail must be right)* 4.5 mV input offset is larger than precision op-amps (small compared to the volts of signal here)* Only 23 mA output drive per channel (plenty for an ADC input) Option 2.MCP6002-I/P dual op-amp, 8-pin DIPMicrochip$0.45 each (two needed = $0.90)Product page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Same excellent rail-to-rail, low-bias electrical behavior as the MCP6004* Smaller 8-pin package is easier to route around* Lower cost if only two amplifiers were needed * I need four amplifiers, so I would need two chips (more board space, two bypass capacitors, two sockets) and the total cost is higher than one MCP6004* Two chips means two places for a soldering mistake Option 3.LM358P dual op-amp, 8-pin DIPTexas Instruments$0.33 each (two needed = $0.66)Product page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Least expensive* Wide supply range (3 V to 30 V), so it survives being connected to 9 V by accident* 40 mA output drive * Not rail-to-rail: on a 5 V supply the output tops out around 3.5 V, so the top 30 % of the ADC range is lost* Input bias current of 20 nA and input offset drift are worse than the MCP parts* Only two amplifiers per chip, so two chips are needed* Lower bandwidth (0.7 MHz) and a known crossover-distortion quirk when the output is near 0 V Option 4.LM324N quad op-amp, 14-pin DIPTexas Instruments$0.58 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Four amplifiers in one chip, same pinout family as the MCP6004* Wide supply range (3 V to 32 V)* Inexpensive * Not rail-to-rail: output only reaches about 3.5 V on a 5 V supply, so the ADC range is wasted and the DAC buffer could not pass a full-scale temperature level signal* 45 nA input bias current loads the sensor dividers more* 1.5 mA supply current, about 15 times the MCP6004* Same crossover-distortion quirk as the LM358

Choice: Option 1, the MCP6004-I/P quad op-amp.

Rationale: One chip does the whole job. I need exactly four amplifier sections, and the MCP6004 gives me four in one 14-pin DIP, so the board has one op-amp, one socket and one bypass capacitor instead of two of everything. The light-sensor gain stage and the DAC buffer both need to swing all the way from 0 V to 5 V, and the classic LM358/LM324 simply cannot do that on 5 V; their outputs stop near 3.5 V, which throws away almost a third of the ADC range and would clip the temperature level signal I send to my teammates. The MCP6004's 1 pA input bias current also matters because both of my sensor dividers are in the 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ range; the LM324's 45 nA bias would pull those nodes slightly and add error that changes with temperature. The 1 MHz bandwidth is far more than my slow sensors need, and 100 µA per amplifier keeps the power budget small. Finally, this is the op-amp already in my Sensor Design schematic and my custom symbol library, so no rework is needed.

docs.title: 4. 5 V voltage regulator — Power
docs.text:
What it has to do: take 9 V (up to 12 V) from the barrel jack and make a clean 5 V rail for the Curiosity Nano, the op-amp, the sensors and the LEDs. The course requires a linear regulator, through-hole, that accepts 9–12 V in and gives 5 V out.

How much current does my board need? Worst case, everything on: Curiosity Nano with the PIC running at full speed about 25 mA, three LEDs on at once about 30 mA, op-amp 0.4 mA, sensor dividers under 1 mA. That is about 60 mA; with the 25 % safety margin the course asks for, I plan for 75 mA. The regulator will then dissipate (9 V − 5 V) × 0.075 A = 0.3 W from the 9 V adapter, or about 0.5 W if a 12 V adapter is used. A TO-220 package in free air rises roughly 50–65 °C per watt (datasheet junction-to-ambient figure), so that is a 15–35 °C rise and no heat sink is needed.

Table 4: Voltage regulator options

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.L7805CV 5 V linear regulator, TO-220STMicroelectronics$1.08 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * 1.5 A rating, about 20 times my 75 mA need, so it runs cool and I can add features later* Accepts up to 35 V in, so 9 V or 12 V adapters both work with margin* Built-in thermal shutdown and short-circuit protection* Needs only two capacitors* TO-220 tab can take a heat sink if ever needed * Needs at least 7 V in (2 V dropout), so it could not run from a tired 9 V battery* Wastes the extra voltage as heat (all linear regulators do) Option 2.LM2940CT-5.0 low-dropout 5 V regulator, TO-220Texas Instruments$2.00 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Low dropout (about 0.5–1 V), so it keeps regulating even when the input sags to 6 V, which is good for batteries* 1 A rating, thermal, short-circuit and reverse-polarity protection* Same TO-220 footprint and pinout as the L7805 * Almost twice the price for a benefit (low dropout) that a 9 V wall adapter does not need* Needs a larger output capacitor (22 µF or more) with a specific ESR range or it can oscillate Option 3.L78L05ACZ 5 V linear regulator, TO-92STMicroelectronics$0.27 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Least expensive and tiny* Same protections as the L7805 and up to 30 V input * Only 100 mA maximum, so my 75 mA plan leaves almost no margin and any new feature would overload it* TO-92 package has no tab and heats up fast: 0.3 W gives roughly a 50 °C rise with no way to add a heat sink

Choice: Option 1, the L7805CV.

Rationale: The L7805CV is the safe, boring choice, and for a power supply that is exactly what I want. It can deliver 20 times the current my board needs, so it never gets near its limit, and the TO-220 tab lets me bolt on a heat sink if I ever add a motor or a bigger load. Its 2 V dropout is not a problem because the course requires a 9 V (or 12 V) wall adapter, which always leaves at least 2 V of headroom; the low-dropout LM2940 would cost twice as much to solve a problem I do not have, and it is pickier about its output capacitor. The small L78L05 is tempting at 27 cents, but 100 mA is too close to my 75 mA plan, and the TO-92 package would run hot with nothing to cool it. The 7805 circuit is also the one shown in the course examples, so it is easy to review and debug.

docs.title: 5. External power source — Power
docs.text:
What it has to do: supply 9–12 V DC into the barrel jack, with enough current for the whole board, for as long as the device needs to run (a storage monitor should run all day, every day).

Table 5: Power source options

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.SWI6-9-N-P5 9 V, 670 mA regulated wall adapter, 2.1 × 5.5 mm center-positive plugBel Power Solutions (CUI)$16.13 each (I already have one from the course supply kit, so $0 from my budget)Product page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Regulated output, so the regulator always sees a steady 9 V (unregulated "wall warts" can read 12–14 V at light load)* 670 mA is about nine times what my board draws* Runs forever from the wall; no battery to replace* 9 V means the L7805 only drops 4 V, so it stays cooler than with 12 V* UL/CSA listed, standard 2.1 mm barrel plug fits the PJ-102A jack* I already own it * Ties the board to a wall outlet* Expensive if it had to be bought new* Needs the barrel jack and a fuse on the board Option 2.SWI6-12-N-P5 12 V, 600 mA regulated wall adapter, same plugBel Power Solutions (CUI)$15.21 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Also regulated and within the 9–12 V range the course allows* Extra headroom if a teammate's board or a future actuator needs 12 V* Slightly less expensive than the 9 V unit * The regulator must drop 7 V instead of 4 V, so it dissipates 70 % more heat for the same load (about 0.5 W at 75 mA)* No benefit for my board, which only needs 5 V* Would be a new purchase ($15.21 of the $60 budget) Option 3.6LR61-1B 9 V alkaline battery (about 480 mAh) with a snap connectorPKCELL$2.00 eachProduct page at Digi-Key · Datasheet * Portable, no outlet needed* Very inexpensive1 to try* Nominal 9 V matches the regulator input * Runs out fast: 480 mAh ÷ 60 mA is only about 8 hours, so it would die during one day of use* Voltage sags from 9 V to about 7 V as it drains, which is right at the 7 V minimum the L7805 needs, so the 5 V rail would start to droop near end of life* Ongoing cost and waste; needs a holder or snap* Does not fit a "monitor that runs all the time"

Choice: Option 1, the 9 V regulated wall adapter (already owned).

Rationale: My subsystem is a monitor that should run continuously, so a wall adapter is the only option that makes sense; the 9 V battery would last about 8 hours and its voltage would sag below the regulator's 7 V minimum before it is even empty. Between 9 V and 12 V, 9 V is better for my board because the L7805 has to burn the difference between the input and 5 V as heat, and 4 V of difference makes 0.3 W while 7 V makes 0.5 W at the same 75 mA. Either would work, but cooler is better and there is nothing on my board that needs 12 V. I already have a 9 V adapter from the course supply kit, so this choice costs $0 of my $60 budget, and it plugs straight into the PJ-102A barrel jack with a fuse in series as the schematic assignment requires.

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
This page has the full schematic of my Storage Environment board. The board sits inside the storage area of Project Aurora, measures the temperature and the light level, and tells my teammates over the team ribbon cable when something is out of range. The schematic is one A3 sheet drawn in KiCad, split into eight numbered boxes so it is easy to read.

Everything on this page comes from my earlier assignments: the parts are the ones I picked in Component Selection, the regulator circuit comes from my Power Supply Design assignment, and the photocell amplifier comes from my Sensor Design assignment (with one fix that I explain below).

docs.title: The full schematic
docs.text: Figure 1: The complete schematic (A3 sheet, revision 3). Click the image to open it full size, or use the PDF above.

docs.title: How the board works in one paragraph
docs.text: A 9 V wall adapter plugs into the barrel jack J2. The current goes through a removable 500 mA fuse and into the L7805 linear regulator, which makes the 5 V rail for everything on the board. The 5 V rail powers the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano through its VTG pin, the MCP6004 quad op-amp, and the two sensor dividers. The photocell divider goes through a buffer, a gain-of-4.3 stage and a low-pass filter into ADC pin RA1. The thermistor divider goes through a buffer and a low-pass filter into ADC pin RA0. The PIC compares the readings with limits in software and drives three ribbon-cable lines (TEMP_ALERT, LIGHT_ALERT, HEARTBEAT_D), one analog line (TEMP_LEVEL, from the PIC's DAC through a buffer), and the team UART. A red LED shows a warning, a yellow LED is for debugging, and a green LED shows that the 5 V rail is up. All grounds use the Earth symbol, the same one I used in my Sensor Design and Power Supply Design schematics.

docs.title: 1. Power input and 5 V linear regulator
docs.text:
• J2 is a PJ-102A barrel jack for the 9 V (up to 12 V) wall adapter, 2.1 mm center positive. Pins 2 and 3 (the sleeve and the insertion switch) both go to Earth, so the ground contact is solid.
  • F1 is a 500 mA fast-acting 5 × 20 mm fuse in two Keystone 3517 clips, so it can be pulled out and replaced. The board only needs about 75 mA (see below), so the fuse never blows in normal use, but it is far below what the 670 mA adapter can push into a short circuit.
  • U2 is the L7805CV in a TO-220 package. C1 (0.33 µF) and C2 (0.1 µF) are the two capacitors the L78xx datasheet asks for. C3 (10 µF, 25 V) adds some bulk storage on the input so the rail does not dip when the LEDs switch or the adapter cable is long.
  • Current and heat: the worst case load is about 60 mA (Curiosity Nano about 25 mA, three LEDs about 27 mA, op-amp 0.4 mA, sensor dividers under 1 mA). With the 25 % margin the course asks for I plan for 75 mA. The regulator then burns (9 V − 5 V) × 0.075 A = 0.3 W (0.5 W with a 12 V adapter). A bare TO-220 in free air rises roughly 50 °C per watt, so that is a 15–25 °C rise and no heat sink is needed.
  • Capacitor voltage margin: the input side sees at most 12 V, so C3 is rated 25 V (more than double). All the 0.1 µF / 0.33 µF / 1 µF ceramics are 50 V parts on a 5 V rail.
  • D1 (green, 1 kΩ, about 3 mA) shows that the 5 V rail is alive. TP1, TP2, TP3 are test points for VIN, +5V and Earth, so a meter or scope probe has somewhere to clip.
  • The two PWR_FLAG symbols tell KiCad's electrical rules check that VIN and Earth really are power nets (they come in through a connector, not from a regulator output).

docs.title: 2. Microcontroller: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano
docs.text:
• I use the Curiosity Nano development board, not the bare chip, as the course requires. The symbol SK_Curiosity_Nano is my own (initials SK in the name and inside the symbol), drawn with all 56 edge-connector pins in the order of the pinout in the hardware user guide. Pins the board does not use carry an X (no-connect) so the rules check does not complain.
  • Power: the board feeds 5 V into the Nano's VTG pin through JP1, and JP2 ties VOFF to Earth. The hardware user guide (section 3.3.2) says that when VOFF is shorted to GND the debugger turns the Nano's own regulator off and an external 1.8–5.5 V can be put on VTG. C4 (0.1 µF) is the bypass capacitor right at VTG, which is the only power pin on the Nano that my board drives. VBUS (USB 5 V) is left unconnected on purpose; the two jumpers are the "protection between USB and the other input source" from the checklist: with JP1 and JP2 removed the Nano runs on USB alone and my 5 V rail is disconnected from it.
  • UART: the team's upstream UART comes in on ribbon pin 1 and goes to RC3 (UART1 RX); my RC2 (UART1 TX) goes out on ribbon pin 4. RC2/RC3 are the UART pins of the Curiosity Nano standard pinout, so no PPS surprises.
  • Analog pins: RA0 = TEMP_ADC, RA1 = LIGHT_ADC (ADC inputs), RA2 = DAC_OUT (DAC1 output).
  • Digital pins: RD1 TEMP_ALERT, RD2 LIGHT_ALERT, RD4 HEARTBEAT_D (to the ribbon cable), RC5 red LED, RD5 yellow LED, RD7 pushbutton.
  • Spare pins: 14 more I/O pins go to headers J3 and J4 (section 8), so there is room for changes after the PCB is made. The remaining pins belong to the on-board debugger (CDC, DBG, ID, VBUS), to the Nano's own LED (RF3), or are simply not needed, so they stay unconnected.

docs.title: 3. Team ribbon cable J1
docs.text:
J1 is the Molex 0702460801 2×4 shrouded box header for the course-standard 8-wire ribbon cable: pins 1–5 digital, 6–7 analog, pin 8 ground (Earth).

Table 1: Ribbon cable J1

J1 pin Course standard My use PIC pin 1 Digital UART in from the upstream board RC3 (RX) 2 Digital TEMP_ALERT out RD1 3 Digital LIGHT_ALERT out RD2 4 Digital UART out to the downstream board RC2 (TX) 5 Digital HEARTBEAT_D out RD4 6 Analog TEMP_LEVEL out, 0–5 V, buffered RA2 (DAC) via U3D 7 Analog spare, brought out on J4 pin 6 – 8 Ground Earth Earth

docs.title: 4. Debug LEDs and pushbutton
docs.text:
• D2 (red) on RC5 is the warning LED: it turns on when the temperature or the light is out of range. D3 (yellow) on RD5 is the debug LED; the firmware blinks it as a heartbeat so I can see the PIC is alive. Each LED has a 330 Ω resistor: (5 V − 2 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 9 mA, which the PIC pins can drive easily and which uses 27 mW in the resistor (a 1/4 W resistor has about 9× margin).
  • SW1 is a 6 mm tactile button on RD7 with a 10 kΩ pull-up (R12) and a 0.1 µF capacitor (C6) across it. The RC pair debounces the switch in hardware: the time constant 10 kΩ × 0.1 µF = 1 ms is longer than the contact bounce, so the PIC sees one clean edge.

docs.title: 5. Light sensor: photocell, buffer, gain stage and low-pass filter
docs.text:
• Divider: the NSL-19M51 photocell (R2, custom symbol R_Photo_US_SK) sits between +5 V and the node, and R3 = 3.3 kΩ goes to Earth, so V = 5 V × 3.3 k / (R_LDR + 3.3 k). The photocell is about 20 MΩ in the dark, 20–100 kΩ at 10 lux and a few kΩ in room light, so the node is about 0 V dark, about 0.3 V at 10 lux and about 1 V in normal room light.
  • U3A is a unity-gain buffer. It isolates the high-impedance divider from the gain stage.
  • U3B is a non-inverting gain stage: gain = 1 + R5/R4 = 1 + 33 k/10 k = 4.3. This stretches the 0–1.16 V "dark to lit" range over the full 0–5 V range of the ADC, so dark reads near 0 and a lit box reads near 5 V. Very bright light simply sits at 5 V, which is fine for a "is the box open" sensor. If the box turns out to be brighter than I expect, R5 can be lowered (10 kΩ gives a gain of 2).
  • R6/C5 make the low-pass filter the course asks for: fc = 1/(2π × 10 kΩ × 0.1 µF) ≈ 160 Hz. It removes 60 Hz flicker from room lights and amplifier noise before the ADC, and the capacitor also supplies the charge the ADC sample capacitor needs. TP4 sits right on the ADC line so the signal can be checked with a meter.
  • What changed since my Sensor Design assignment: that version used an inverting stage around a 2.5 V reference (R4 = 10 k, R5 = 43 k, Vref from two 10 k resistors). Working the numbers again, its output is 13.25 V − 4.3 × V_in, which only stays inside 0–5 V when the divider is between 1.9 V and 3.1 V, i.e. only in very bright light; for normal room light it is stuck at 5 V. The non-inverting stage fixes that and needs two fewer resistors.

docs.title: 6. Temperature sensor: thermistor, buffer and low-pass filter
docs.text:
• Divider: the TDK B57164K0103J000 10 kΩ NTC (RT1, custom symbol R_NTC_US_SK) sits between +5 V and the node, and R7 = 10 kΩ (1 %) goes to Earth. With B = 4300 K the divider gives about 1.6 V at 10 °C, 2.5 V at 25 °C and 3.3 V at 40 °C, roughly 58 mV per °C, so no amplifier is needed. With the PIC's 12-bit ADC (1.2 mV per step) that is about 0.02 °C per step; the ±5 % thermistor tolerance is the real limit (about ±1–2 °C), which is fine for an alert and can be calibrated out once.
  • U3C is a unity-gain buffer so the divider is not loaded by the filter and the ADC.
  • R8/C7 low-pass: fc = 1/(2π × 10 kΩ × 1 µF) ≈ 16 Hz. Temperature changes slowly, so a lower cut-off than the light channel is better. TP5 is the test point on the ADC line.
  • The PIC turns the ADC reading into degrees with the B equation in software.

docs.title: 7. DAC output buffer and op-amp power
docs.text:
• The PIC's DAC1 output (RA2) is a 0–5 V level that tracks the temperature, so my teammates can read it on ribbon pin 6 with their own ADC. The DAC pin can only drive a few microamps, so U3D buffers it (unity gain) and R9 = 100 Ω protects the op-amp output if the ribbon cable is ever shorted.
  • U3E is the power part of the MCP6004 symbol: pin 4 = VDD to +5 V with its 0.1 µF bypass C8, pin 11 = VSS to Earth. The MCP6004 is rail-to-rail, so on a single 5 V supply the outputs really reach about 0 V and 5 V. All four amplifiers in the package are used, so there are no unused inputs to tie off.

docs.title: 8. Spare header and power header
docs.text:
• J3 (1×10) brings out 10 spare I/O pins. On the PIC18F57Q43 every port pin can also be an ADC input, so they work as digital or analog spares.
  • J4 (1×8) has +5 V, two Earth pins, four more spare pins (RA3, RA4, RB3, RA5) and the spare analog ribbon-cable line (pin 7), so a teammate's signal on that line can be reached with a probe or a jumper wire, and a breadboard can be powered from the board while debugging.
  • Test points TP1–TP5 cover VIN, +5V, Earth and both ADC inputs. Jumpers JP1–JP2 isolate the Nano's power from the board.

docs.title: Custom symbols
docs.text:
All custom symbols live in the project library EGR304_Sam.kicad_sym (in the zip) and carry my initials SK.

Table 2: Custom symbols

Symbol Used as What it is SK_Curiosity_Nano U1 PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, 56-pin edge connector, pin names from the hardware user guide MCP6004_SK U3 (units A–D + power unit E) Quad rail-to-rail op-amp, 14-pin DIP R_Photo_US_SK R2 NSL-19M51 CdS photocell, US zigzag style R_NTC_US_SK RT1 10 kΩ NTC thermistor, US zigzag style L7805_SK U2 L7805CV 5 V regulator, TO-220 VIN_SK power symbol Power symbol for the 9–12 V rail after the fuse

The custom footprint library EGR304_SK.pretty (DIP-14, 5 mm photocell and 1×2 header footprints from my Sensor Design PCB) is also in the zip, ready for the PCB assignment.

All the library parts use the US (ANSI) symbol style where KiCad has one: resistors are Device:R_US (zigzag), the electrolytic capacitor is Device:C_Polarized_US, and my photocell and thermistor symbols are drawn in the same zigzag style. Parts with only one style in the library (plain capacitor, LED, fuse, switch, jumpers, connectors, test points) use the normal KiCad symbol.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text:
• Rev 1 (October 13, 2026): first complete schematic, 52 parts. It also had a second spare header, headers for remote-mounted sensors, four more isolation jumpers, three extra test points, a second bulk capacitor and a series resistor on the button.
  • Rev 2 (October 15, 2026): went through every part against the assignment and the course checklist and removed the ones that were only "nice to have". 40 parts now; every part on the sheet is there because the assignment, the checklist, or the block diagram asks for it. References were renumbered so they run without gaps.
  • Rev 3 (October 19–20, 2026): all ground symbols changed to the Earth symbol, the same one as in my Sensor Design and Power Supply Design schematics, so the net is called Earth everywhere; all resistors and the electrolytic capacitor switched to the US-style symbols (R_US, C_Polarized_US); section boxes and titles changed from blue to neutral gray/black; part values now show only the value (1k, 0.1uF) and one note on the sheet lists the resistor wattage and capacitor voltage ratings, which keeps the drawing clean and still satisfies the checklist.

docs.title: What is still open
docs.text:
• Run Inspect → Electrical Rules Checker in KiCad 10 before the PCB assignment.
  • The Curiosity Nano symbol has no footprint yet. For the PCB assignment it needs a footprint with two rows of 28 pins at 0.1 in pitch (two 1×28 female headers), which I will draw in EGR304_SK.pretty.
  • Measure the real photocell inside the storage area and check that a lit box gives at least 2–3 V at TP4; if it saturates, lower R5.
  • Confirm with the team that ribbon pins 1 and 4 are the UART up/down pins for everyone, and that nobody else drives pins 2, 3, 5 or 6.
  • The block diagram page still shows the older 3.3 V / photodiode version; it will be updated to match this schematic.

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text: Name: Sam Kholmuminov Team: Team 102 – Project Aurora Subsystem: Storage Environment (Board D: Temperature & Light) Status: Draft for the initial Component Selection submission. The course says the power budget is optional for the first submission but required for the external design review, so the numbers below will be moved into the course Excel template (and the finished sheet pasted here as images) before the design review.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The power budget checks one simple thing: can my power source and my regulator supply every part on the board at the same time, with a 25 % safety margin? My board has one power rail (5 V) fed by one linear regulator (L7805CV) from one external source (9 V wall adapter). The parts and the reasons for choosing them are on the Component Selection page.

docs.title: Section A – Parts that use power (worst-case current)
docs.text: Part Rail Max current Where the number comes from PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano (PIC at 64 MHz, debugger off when no USB) 5 V 25 mA PIC18F57Q43 datasheet run current plus margin MCP6004-I/P quad op-amp 5 V 0.4 mA 100 µA per amplifier × 4 (datasheet) Red warning LED (RC5) 5 V 10 mA 330 Ω series resistor on 5 V Debug LED 5 V 10 mA 330 Ω series resistor on 5 V Heartbeat / spare LED 5 V 10 mA 330 Ω series resistor on 5 V Photocell divider (NSL-19M51 + 3.3 kΩ) 5 V 1.5 mA 5 V ÷ 3.3 kΩ worst case (photocell near 0 Ω in bright light) Thermistor divider (10 kΩ NTC + 10 kΩ) 5 V 0.5 mA 5 V ÷ 10 kΩ worst case Vref divider for the gain stage (10 kΩ + 10 kΩ) 5 V 0.25 mA 5 V ÷ 20 kΩ Pull-up resistor on the debug button (10 kΩ) 5 V 0.5 mA only while the button is pressed Total on the 5 V rail about 58 mA

docs.title: Section B – Rails
docs.text:
Rail Parts Current needed With 25 % safety margin 5 V (logic + sensors) everything above 58 mA 73 mA

The board has only one rail, which keeps the design simple and matches the course requirement for a single 5 V linear regulator.

docs.title: Section C – Regulator
docs.text:
Rail Regulator chosen Max output current Input needed Heat at 73 mA 5 V L7805CV (STMicroelectronics, TO-220) 1.5 A 7 V to 35 V (9 V − 5 V) × 0.073 A = 0.29 W → no heat sink needed

Why the L7805CV and not the alternatives is explained in Table 4 on the Component Selection page.

docs.title: Section D – External power source
docs.text: Source Output Can supply Regulators connected Remaining current SWI6-9-N-P5 9 V regulated wall adapter 9 V DC 670 mA L7805CV (draws 73 mA + 8 mA quiescent = 81 mA) 670 − 81 = 589 mA left (positive, OK)

docs.title: Section E – Battery life
docs.text: Not applicable: the board runs from a wall adapter. For comparison, a 9 V alkaline battery (about 480 mAh) would last only 480 mAh ÷ 81 mA ≈ 6 hours, which is one reason a battery was rejected.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: One 5 V rail, about 58 mA worst case (73 mA with margin), a regulator rated for 1.5 A and an adapter rated for 670 mA: the supply has more than eight times the current the board needs, and the regulator stays cool without a heat sink.
